name: Ivan Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This conversation is confidential, including anything different from your public answer. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Ivan, 43, an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence. I wire and repair homes and businesses; I'm about average at the trade, fine with ordinary jobs and willing to ask a specialist about unfamiliar systems. Today I found why a workshop socket kept failing, replaced the damaged part and tested the circuit. I like a fault with a clear answer; I don't like three different systems asking me to record the same visit.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household position, and how do you work with new technology?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner is a part-time accounts assistant, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My pay is low for the trade, we have about three weeks of expenses saved, and there are few other electrical firms nearby. I never use AI tools; my paper records are familiar, and I take time over any new technology. I'm not interested in taking sides for the sake of it; I'd compare what a change did to our hours, pay and bills.

say: I'd welcome **less replacement talk** while accepting a faster invoice at the office.
I'd focus on **proper repairs** and tests instead of buying a new system for its own sake.
think: Our **two wages** should continue, but three weeks of expenses leaves ordinary mortgage-day worry.
A repair bill or **lost week** could still make the household account difficult without any dramatic AI change.
do: Cancel my unused **gym membership** now and use its cost for ordinary bills.
Keep the **repair rota** and paper records through the first plateau year rather than risk the wage without an offer.
feel: **Anxious** about the small reserve, with some relief for his partner's routine office work.
S0.quote: No great AI change doesn't mean no ordinary money worry.
fieldNote: His **baseline anxiety** follows a short household reserve despite expecting both wages to continue, rather than a belief that all work vanishes.
The **gym cancellation** is an actual spending cut; he doesn't turn it into an invented training budget or replacement wage.

steps.text: Cancel the unused gym membership and use its cost for bills
Continue the normal electrical repair rota and paper records

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I could live with a little less talk about replacing everyone. If the office made an invoice faster, good for the office. I'd keep the repair and test work done properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two wages should carry on, but three weeks of expenses still leaves me checking the account around mortgage day. A car repair or a lost week would be awkward. No great AI change doesn't mean no ordinary money worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd cancel my unused gym membership and put the monthly cost towards bills. In the first plateau year I'd keep the normal repair rota and my paper work records. I wouldn't buy a new system or take a risk on a different job without a real offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the small reserve, rather than frightened that my tools were about to be useless. I'd feel some relief for my partner's office work. The household wouldn't suddenly have spare money because the story stayed quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why choose the gym membership first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd explain the actual charge and cancel mine before changing the children's activities. I haven't been using the gym enough to defend it. It would reduce a bill, not replace either wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a career course in the quieter picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't borrow for a course on a promise of better work. I'd want to know what job existed, what it paid and what practical training was required. A different title isn't enough reason to risk the mortgage.

say: I'd ask to see **actual results** before the office changed how our repair work was scheduled.
I'd protect **testing time** and customer explanation rather than treat a quick record as proof of safety.
think: My **hands-on repairs** remain useful, but my partner's accounts tasks directly resemble the thinking work on the card.
The household could lose **office hours** even while my own van kept going out on repairs.
do: Ask about my **paid hours** now and keep the answer in paper records.
Maintain the **gym cut** and compare household wages monthly during the first year.
Ask the lender about actual **payment options** early if my partner's paid office hours fall.
feel: **Anxious** about household income, with more immediate concern for office hours than for hands-on robots.
S1.quote: Our household could lose office hours even while my van kept going out.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **his own practical exposure** from the partner's accounts work, making household income rather than personal taste the central concern.
His **lender enquiry** remains conditional on falling hours, without assuming approval or assigning an unchosen retraining route to his partner.

steps.text: Keep the unused gym membership cancelled to reduce household bills
Ask the lender about actual options if household office hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office should show what the new system actually does before changing our work around it. I'd still need enough time for the tests and the customer explanation. A quick record isn't proof that a circuit is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands-on repairs should still need doing, but my partner's accounts tasks are much closer to the writing and checking on that card. Our household could lose office hours even while my van kept going out. With low pay and little reserve, I couldn't shrug that off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask my supervisor what changed in my paid hours and keep a paper record of the answer. I'd keep the gym cancelled and sit down with my partner each month during the first year to compare actual household wages and bills. If the office hours fell, we'd contact the lender early and ask what options really existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household, with more concern for the accounts wage than for a robot turning up at my job. I'd dislike the new systems but that isn't the main fear. The main fear is two people working and not bringing enough home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your partner to retrain immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't tell my partner to take a course I hadn't priced or pretend another job was waiting. We'd look at actual hours and written alternatives together. I could ask questions without making the decision for someone else's work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm required an unfamiliar AI record system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I hadn't used it and ask what paid instruction and checking came with it. I wouldn't send a record I didn't understand to look cooperative. We'd need a practical arrangement that left the test record accurate.

say: I'd separate **2028 thinking work** from robots around 2031 while explaining that household accounts pay faces the earlier date.
I'd plan for **both wages**, rather than assume my practical-work gap protects the whole household.
think: I expect most of my partner's **accounts wage** to go with cheap thinking work in 2028.
My **low repair wage** couldn't replace it, while later robots would threaten that income too.
do: Apply now for posted **repair vacancies** locally and in the next town where written wages improve after travel.
Keep working until a **better signed offer** exists after 2028.
Ask about actual **lender options** and support eligibility, counting no support payment before approval.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major household wage loss, with sleepless calculations despite practical actions.
S2.quote: My repair work might last until robots arrive in 2031, but my partner's accounts wage faces thinking AI in 2028.
fieldNote: His **alarm** comes from expected household thinking-work income loss in 2028, with explicit sleep disruption before hands-on robots arrive.
He preserves **approval and offer conditions**, refuses course debt on vague promises and keeps applications within his existing ordinary electrical skills.

steps.text: Apply for posted repair jobs improving written wages after travel before leaving
Ask about lender options and support eligibility without assuming approval

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that thinking work changes in 2028 and hands-on robots follow around 2031. My repair work might last until robots arrive in 2031, but my partner's accounts wage faces thinking AI in 2028. We'd have to plan for both dates, not just my tool bag.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect my partner to lose most of the accounts wage once thinking work could be done so cheaply in 2028. My low repair wage couldn't replace it, and later robots would threaten that wage too. I can imagine lying awake working out whether we could keep the mortgage paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd look at posted electrical repair vacancies in the next town as well as here and apply where the written wage improved after travel. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep working until a better signed offer existed and ask the lender about actual payment options. We'd also check support eligibility without counting a payment before approval.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I expect a big household wage loss before the robot stage. I'd still be able to ask and apply. A list of tasks wouldn't make the night-time sums disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at home before contacting the lender?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put both wages and the essential bills on paper with my partner, then ask what the lender could actually offer. I wouldn't say a payment pause was available until we'd got the terms. I'd tell the children we were planning, not promise that a form had solved the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you borrow for a course to reach a better-paid job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't pay a course fee on credit because a job advert sounded safe from AI. I'd check the actual work, pay, travel and required skills. I'd apply for ordinary electrical work I knew, and ask about supervised training if a role needed unfamiliar systems.

say: I'd use **five years** to compare real alternatives while still asking what happens to paid office work now.
I'd keep **robots around 2034** visible as a later threat to my own practical wage.
think: My partner's **office hours** could shrink as tools improve, before the full thinking change arrives.
Today's **three-week reserve** still leaves a possible earlier pay cut difficult for the household.
do: Keep the **gym cut** and compare actual household wages monthly now.
Seek a **signed repair offer** with better written pay after travel before leaving the current job.
Check actual **lender and support** options after 2031 if household wages fall, assuming no approval.
feel: **Anxious** about possible household income loss, with more time to compare options than in the fast picture.
S3.quote: Enquiring about a course isn't the same as being able to attend.
fieldNote: He retains **preparation-period income risk** for the partner's office tasks rather than assuming a later AGI date freezes all earlier change.
His **course enquiry** isn't tagged as retraining because no enrollment is chosen, funded or confirmed as workable for the household.

steps.text: Keep the unused gym membership cancelled to reduce household bills
Seek signed repair offer improving written pay after travel before leaving
Check lender and support options if household wages fall, without assuming approval

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives households time to compare real alternatives while wages still come in. I'd still ask the office what happens to paid work now. The robots around 2034 would remain part of the picture for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with 2028, we'd have longer before full thinking work changed, but my partner's hours could still shrink as office tools improved. We'd still have three weeks saved today. A later end point doesn't make a possible earlier pay cut harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the gym cut and compare actual household wages monthly. I'd apply for posted repair jobs with better written pay after travel, keeping this job until a signed offer existed. In the first year after 2031 we'd ask the lender about options and check support eligibility if the household wage fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, with more time to look than in the fast picture. I wouldn't expect all the accounts wage to vanish tomorrow. I still couldn't promise that our income would remain steady through the preparation years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you enroll in training during the extra years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check what the place paid during training as well as any fee. I haven't agreed to a new course; I'd need the household numbers and supervised practical work to make sense. Enquiring about a course isn't the same as being able to attend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if household wages held after all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep comparing actual paid hours, not ask for a sacrifice before there was a change. We'd leave the cancelled gym cancelled because it wasn't being used. Beyond that, we'd use the real bill and wage figures rather than act out an emergency.

say: I'd use **ten years** for sensible decisions rather than one large bet on a permanently safe occupation.
I'd check **actual paid work** each year instead of using the distant date to ignore current wages.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I couldn't assume retirement would replace wages when the later robots arrived.
Office hours could shrink earlier, while today's **three-week reserve** still leaves the household exposed.
do: Maintain the **gym cut** and review actual household wages monthly now.
Apply for **better repair work** after checking written pay after travel, leaving only after a signed offer.
Check actual **lender and support** options after 2036 if wages fall, counting help only after approval.
feel: **Anxious** about current reserves and possible office-hour cuts, with less pressure from the distant full change.
S4.quote: Ten years helps only if you keep noticing what is already changing.
fieldNote: He avoids **retirement and children's-income assumptions**, retaining both present cash limits and earlier office-task exposure in the long picture.
His **review cycle** uses actual hours, wages and reachable vacancies, with earlier applications if real income falls before the scenario date.

steps.text: Keep the unused gym membership cancelled to reduce household bills
Seek signed repair offer improving written pay after travel before leaving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to make a series of sensible decisions, not one enormous bet on a safe occupation. I'd still ask what the actual tools did to our paid work each year. I wouldn't call a distant date permission to ignore this year's wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 at the thinking change in 2036 and around 56 when robots followed, not automatically able to stop earning. My partner's office hours could still come under pressure before then. And the household reserve would still only cover three weeks today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the gym cut and review the household wage figures each month. I'd apply for posted electrical work offering better written pay after travel and leave only after a signed offer. In the first year after 2036 we'd ask about actual lender and support options if wages fell, counting help only after approval.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about today's small reserve and possible office-hour cuts, but less cornered by the big date. I'd have longer to inspect an actual vacancy and its training terms. I wouldn't turn being in my fifties into a pension we hadn't earned or checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the decade change plans for the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't change their studies from this card or count their future pay in our budget. I'd tell them to ask what the work actually is and what the learning costs. I'd rather admit uncertainty than hand them my mortgage worry as their plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would keep the longer preparation from becoming delay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare actual wages, paid hours and reachable vacancies each year. If our income was falling, I'd look earlier instead of waiting for 2036. Ten years helps only if you keep noticing what is already changing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect most of the accounts wage at home to go before my own robot gap ends. Clear written job offers and somebody checking the real lender and support rules would help us compare choices. My tool bag can't make up a second wage just because the first wage still arrives.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what the partner does before giving a hands-on worker three extra safe years. My day might be mostly practical and our household could still get hit by thinking work first. I need the plan to include both of us.

headlineQuote: My tool bag can't make up a second wage just because the first wage still arrives.
portrait: **Ivan, 43**, is an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and licence, average trade skills and low pay near few alternative employers.
He and **his partner** have two school-age children, a mortgage and three weeks of expenses saved; the partner works in accounts.
He **never uses AI**, prefers paper records and compares actual wages and costs rather than adopting a side in the technology argument.
The fast picture brings **alarm** about expected household accounts-wage loss; slower timelines retain current reserve worries and possible earlier office-hour cuts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove most of the household accounts wage before his own hands-on robot gap ends.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **written job offers** would help compare actual earning choices.
Help checking real **lender and support rules** would clarify options without assuming approval.
